summary: DMARC lets the owner of an email's Author Domain state how receivers should handle messages that fail validation, and request reports about use of the domain. Receivers can use this when deciding what to do with mail. This Standards Track document obsoletes RFC 7489 and RFC 9091.

eli5.summary: A school tells mailmen: "If a letter claims to be from us but looks fake, throw it out, and tell us about it."

questions: where is the dmarc record published
subtitle: How a domain owner tells receivers which email really comes from its name, what to do with the rest, and where to send reports.

tldr.problem: Abusive email often fakes the domain in the From header field of a message, a domain the recipient is expected to trust. SPF and DKIM authenticate domains, but not directly the domain people see in From.
tldr.mechanism: The domain owner publishes a DMARC Policy Record, a DNS TXT record at _dmarc plus the domain name. A receiver checks that an SPF or DKIM domain that passed is aligned with the From domain, then may use the owner's stated handling preference and send back reports.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9989 is a Standards Track document that obsoletes RFC 7489 and RFC 9091. It adds a DNS Tree Walk for finding the organizational domain and says receivers must not reject mail solely because of p=reject.

facts.label: DNS record
facts.value: TXT record at the _dmarc label under the domain

today: RFC 9989 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2026. It obsoletes RFC 7489 and RFC 9091, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it in the unit metadata.

sections.title: The Problem DMARC Addresses
sections.content:
Abusive email often makes unauthorized and deceptive use of a domain name in the From header field, which the RFC calls RFC5322.From. That domain is usually one the recipient knows and presumably trusts. SPF (RFC 7208) and DKIM (RFC 6376) provide domain-level authentication, but neither is directly tied to the domain in From, called the Author Domain.

DMARC fills that gap. The domain owner publishes a DNS TXT record describing its authentication policy for the Author Domain and asking for particular handling of messages that fail validation. The result is a plain pass or fail.

A DMARC pass only means that use of the Author Domain was validated as authorized by the Domain Owner. It does not say the message is safe or desirable. A failure does not prove the message is unauthorized either, so a receiver may honor the requested handling but is not required to do so.

DMARC is deliberately narrow. It targets exact-domain spoofing. It does not address look-alike domain names or tricks in the human-readable display name, and it does not look at message content.
sections.eli5: Anyone can write any return address on an envelope. DMARC lets the real owner of a name say how to check that a letter with that name is genuine.

sections.title: Identifier Alignment
sections.content:
DMARC does not accept just any SPF or DKIM pass. A message gets a DMARC pass only if a domain that was authenticated by SPF or DKIM is aligned with the Author Domain. Without this, a bad actor could sign mail with its own domain, or publish its own SPF record, and pass those checks while writing someone else's name in From.

There are two alignment modes. In relaxed alignment the two domains need the same Organizational Domain, the domain at the top of the namespace hierarchy that has the same administrative authority. In strict alignment they must be identical. The default for both is relaxed, and the Domain Owner chooses the mode in its policy record.

For SPF, DMARC relies solely on the validated MAIL FROM identity. For DKIM, the identifier is the domain in the d tag of a validated signature. A message with several DKIM signatures passes if any one of them aligns. The RFC recommends that Domain Owners use both SPF and DKIM.

Messages without a single, properly formed RFC5322.From header field cannot be aligned, and handling them is outside the scope of the specification.
sections.eli5: Imagine a letter that says it is from "Mia at Smith School". The post office checks that the stamp really came from Smith School, not just from some school. The two names have to match, either exactly or at least both from the same school.

sections.title: The DMARC Policy Record
sections.content:
A DMARC Policy Record is a DNS TXT record published at the name made by putting the label _dmarc in front of the domain. For example.com it lives at _dmarc.example.com. It uses the tag-value syntax from DKIM, and unknown tags MUST be ignored.

The v tag is required, MUST come first and must be exactly DMARC1; otherwise the whole record is ignored. The main tags are:

  • p: the Domain Owner Assessment Policy for mail that fails validation (none, quarantine or reject). If it is missing, the record is treated as p=none.
  • sp and np: the policy for existing subdomains and for non-existent subdomains.
  • adkim and aspf: relaxed (r) or strict (s) alignment, default r.
  • rua and ruf: where to send aggregate reports and per-message failure reports. A receiver that sends reports MUST support mailto: URIs, and with no tag it MUST NOT generate that kind of report.
  • psd and t: whether a domain is a Public Suffix Domain, and a test-mode flag that asks receivers to apply a policy one level softer.

A domain that is only collecting data uses p=none and is said to be in Monitoring Mode. A policy that is not none across the organizational domain and its subdomains is called Enforcement.
sections.eli5: The record is a little note taped to the front door of the domain. It says which stamps count, what to do with letters that fail the check, and where to mail reports about them.

sections.title: Policy Discovery and the DNS Tree Walk
sections.content:
A receiver first asks for the record at _dmarc plus the Author Domain. If there is none, it performs a DNS Tree Walk: it removes the left-most label step by step and queries each parent name for a valid record. Records that do not start with the current version tag are discarded, and if several records come back for one name, all are discarded. The walk stops at a record containing psd=n or psd=y.

The walk also finds the Organizational Domain. This replaces the Public Suffix List approach of RFC 7489, which required no specific list and gave no guidance on how often to refresh it. A psd=n record marks an Organizational Domain; a psd=y record from a Public Suffix Operator means the Organizational Domain is one label below it; otherwise the record found with the fewest labels wins.

To stop abuse of long names, an Author Domain with more than eight labels causes no more than eight queries. If a record is wanted for such a long name, the owner MUST publish it at that exact name, because that name is always queried first.

If no record exists at all, the receiver MUST NOT apply DMARC. How DNS errors are handled is up to the receiver, who may fail open or fail closed.
sections.eli5: If a house has no sign, you check the street, then the neighborhood, then the town, until you find someone who has posted the rules. There is a limit on how far up you go, so nobody can send you walking forever.

sections.title: What Domain Owners and Receivers Do
sections.content:
A Domain Owner sets up SPF and DKIM so mail produces an authenticated domain aligned with the Author Domain, creates a mailbox for aggregate reports, and then publishes a record. Owners usually start at p=none with a rua address, read the reports, fix legitimate mail streams that fail, and only then decide on enforcement. The RFC notes this can take many months. Remediation MUST happen before moving to enforcement.

A Public Suffix Operator that publishes a record MUST include psd=y.

A Mail Receiver extracts the Author Domain, discovers the policy, collects the SPF and DKIM results, checks alignment and decides pass or fail. One or more aligned identifiers make a pass; none makes a fail. It keeps the results for reports and SHOULD send aggregate reports at least once every 24 hours. Failure reports are optional, and many receivers redact them or skip them for privacy.

What happens to a failing message is always local policy. Receivers MAY accept mail even when the policy is reject, SHOULD add an Authentication-Results header field, and SHOULD report any deviation through the PolicyOverride feature of the aggregate report. A policy of p=none MUST NOT change existing mail handling.
sections.eli5: The school first checks that its own letters carry the right stamp, then watches the reports for a while, and only later tells the post office to throw away fakes. The post office decides in the end what to do.

sections.title: Mailing Lists, Forwarding and p=reject
sections.content:
A strict policy breaks some legitimate mail. Forwarders such as alumni addresses and role-based aliases usually fail SPF because the relay's IP address is not authorized by the original domain, while DKIM signatures generally survive. So a domain that publishes p=reject MUST NOT rely solely on SPF.

Mailing lists are the harder case. Domains with general users who post to lists SHOULD NOT publish p=reject. A domain that wants to should first publish p=none for at least a month, then p=quarantine for as long, and compare the results.

Receivers MUST NOT reject incoming mail solely because of a p=reject policy; without other knowledge they MUST treat such mail as if the policy were p=quarantine. Rejecting list mail can even get a subscriber automatically unsubscribed.

The RFC records that mailing list software has all adopted workarounds that make the From header line aligned, and that methods such as ARC (RFC 8617) have not become widely used. For more on the problem see RFC 7960.
sections.eli5: If a letter is passed along by a friend, the stamp may look wrong even though the letter is real. So the post office should not always throw such letters away.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
DMARC is only as strong as SPF, DKIM and the DNS beneath it. An overly permissive source can obtain a pass the owner never intended, and an attacker who can forge DNS responses can make aligned mail look unaligned or the reverse. The RFC points to DNSSEC, DNS over TLS and DNS over HTTPS as mitigations.

Relaxed alignment has a specific risk: whoever controls the SPF or DKIM records of a subdomain can generate mail that passes on behalf of the organizational domain. Owners should be careful about delegating subdomains and consider strict alignment. Display name attacks are out of scope.

Messages with more than one From domain are outside the specification and are an attack vector; limiting how many Author Domains a receiver processes avoids denial of service.

Reports can leak information. Aggregate reports can reveal sending patterns, especially for small organizations, and failure reports can expose specific users and even message content. DMARC Policy Records for multi-organizational PSDs MUST NOT include ruf.
sections.eli5: The system trusts the phone book (DNS) and the stamps, so those must be protected. Also, the reports are like postcards that could show who writes to whom, so they have to be kept private.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 7489 and RFC 9091
sections.content:
RFC 7489 was an Informational document published through the Independent Submissions Editor. RFC 9989 is an Internet Standards Track document and obsoletes both RFC 7489 and the experimental public suffix extension, RFC 9091.

Tags added: np (imported from RFC 9091), psd and t. Tags removed: pct, rf and ri. The RFC explains that pct was rarely applied accurately except at 0 or 100, and that t replaces some of its function.

The Organizational Domain is now found by the DNS Tree Walk instead of a Public Suffix List. The Domain Owner Actions section is greatly expanded, and the reporting format is moved into separate documents, RFC 9990 for aggregate reports and RFC 9991 for failure reports.
sections.eli5: This is the second, grown-up edition of the rulebook. Some old rules were dropped, a few new ones were added, and the reporting rules got their own books.

items.label: No preference
items.desc: The Domain Owner offers no expression of preference.

items.label: Suspicious
items.desc: The mail is considered suspicious, though it may be valid.

items.label: Not valid
items.desc: Failures are a clear sign the use of the domain name is not valid.
